Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

lexsync (development version)

Upgrading from the previous release (0.1.1)

Changed results

  • matching.tie_break defaults to hash, a keyed hash of each word, where spelling broke ties in favour of early-alphabet words, so designs with ties select different items. matching.tie_break: bytes restores the 0.1.1 tie-break, except under optimal.
  • Generated experiments present one counterbalancing version to each participant, where every list ran in one session, so each Latin-square target appeared in both conditions and a resampled design showed every replicate.
  • A response event after a text event opens its window at the text’s onset, and a response ends the trial, where the window opened once the text had gone and earlier keys were discarded. from: offset restores the delayed window.
  • The PsychoPy and OpenSesame experiments record each reading time and each response with its reaction time and, when the trial has an answer, its accuracy, where they recorded none.
  • In all three targets, a reaction time runs from the stimulus’s onset, or from the response window under from: offset, where jsPsych timed it from the blank response screen.
  • The loop tables give each word and pseudoword trial of a lexical decision its correct key in answer, by default the response event’s first key for word and its second for pseudoword, where the main trials could not be scored.
  • The jsPsych page names each trial’s answer as the browser names the key, such as arrowleft for left, where its feedback called a correct arrow-key press incorrect.
  • Matching leaves out candidates that lack a matched value, in every method, where an anchor without one was paired with the alphabetically first candidate, joint filled a shortfall with incomplete pairs and continuous selection took items without the predictor.
  • counterbalance() applies the paradigm’s Latin square to a design that lists its own events, where it dealt the items factorially and so showed each target in both conditions of a list. counterbalance.recipe: factorial restores the old lists.
  • optimal matching selects the n pairs of least summed distance when the conditions do not overlap (Volgenant, 2004), where it kept the n cheapest pairs of a complete assignment, which did not minimise their summed distance.
  • mahalanobis matching estimates the correlations from the rows complete on the matched dimensions, where a dimension with any missing value lost all its correlations and entered the distance as an independent term.
  • run_pipeline() applies reference_words to a corpus or pool design, recomputing N, OLD20 and any bigram frequency against the list, where it kept the lexicon’s own columns while the datasheet recorded the list as applied.
  • A norms entry’s on: is read as its join key, with a note in the run log, where YAML read a bare on as true and every join used word. Write join_on:.
  • Under the C locale, design, schema and registry files are read in full, where a file was cut at its first accented letter with a warning, so a design could run without its later keys, such as match_on.
  • Generated OpenSesame experiments prepare each display before the trial and time each event from its onset, where every event overran its duration. They log the frame period and send the 254 and 255 session markers.
  • Generated OpenSesame experiments show stimulus text as written, where OpenSesame converted the loop table’s cells, so ‘007’ was shown as 7 and, in OpenSesame 4, ‘True’ as 1.
  • The PsychoPy and OpenSesame experiments hold each trigger code for triggers.trigger_hold_ms, and at least 10 ms, unless the next onset’s code replaces it, where OpenSesame sent a 10 ms pulse.
  • In PsychoPy, the session markers and the code of an event shorter than the hold last the whole hold, where the markers were cleared at once and the event’s code was cut short.
  • The PsychoPy experiment holds the self-paced reading critical-region code for triggers.trigger_hold_ms, where it held it for triggers.inter_trigger_ms, 10 ms by default.
  • When item codes go with condition codes or a design’s own codes from 40 to 239, they skip those codes, where they could coincide, as sets 65 and 66 of a 70-set design took condition codes 101 and 102.
  • A response or question key given alone is written as a list of one key, where jsonlite wrote a bare string, which the PsychoPy runner split into letters.
  • An unquoted y or n in a design is text, where it was TRUE or FALSE, so keys: [y, n] waited for keys named TRUE and FALSE.
  • YAML keys are read by exact name, where a longer key was read in place of an absent one, so a design with font_size: 40 and no font set the font of all three experiments to ‘40’.
  • The PsychoPy experiment runs full screen, and OpenSesame text is 48 pixels high, where it was 32. In the schema, presentation.fullscreen: false restores the 1280 by 1024 window, and presentation.text_height_px sets the text height of all three targets.
  • The English example lexicon en_example.csv holds 3,000 forms screened against SUBTLEX-US, with N and OLD20 counted over the forms kept, where a quarter of its forms were non-standard, mostly names and acronyms, so code that reads it gives different numbers.
  • The English demonstration designs select from the screened en_v2.csv, leave out a list of taboo words and abbreviations and check their pseudowords against wordfreq’s fuller English list, so they select different items.
  • Both apps open on the screened en_v2 lexicon and keep its unmarked forms, so their defaults select different words. Choosing en under ‘Lexicon’ restores the old lexicon.
  • The Shiny app’s presets set their matched dimensions and method, where choosing a preset left ‘Match on’ at length, N and OLD20, so the neighbourhood and 2x2 presets matched on N, which they manipulate.
  • The Shiny app writes a conditions-table edit into the edited cell, where it wrote it one column to the left, so a condition ran with values that were not typed. A typed second-factor bound is kept as a number.
  • Pseudoword generation substitutes every letter the reference attests, where it used a to z and skipped words with other letters, so a generated Spanish design, for example, selects different items. An alphabet of a to z restores make_pseudoword()’s old letters.
  • The words and keys of lexica, pools, norm tables and item tables are put in Unicode NFC as read, so an accented word’s precomposed and decomposed spellings are one word, where both could be selected.
  • CSV values such as t, T, F, 1,000 and ISO dates are text, as in the Python engine, where they were logical, numeric or dates.
  • Each plain decimal in a CSV file is read as its nearest double, which readr could miss by one unit in the last place, and -0 as 0.
  • CSV columns are typed from every row, where readr typed them from the first 1,000 rows, so a later value of another type was read as missing with a warning.
  • Under the C locale, non-ASCII condition labels give the trial order, list balancing and jitter of the Python engine, where they were hashed as escape text.
  • A fractional duration_ms is rounded where it was truncated, so 33.7 ms is presented as 34 ms, and fractional durations read from an item column are rounded in the stimuli and loop tables and counted in the run log.
  • cohens_d(), and the d of cohens_d_ci(), are NA for a condition with fewer than two items, where they were 0, a perfect balance.
  • count_syllables() counts the vowels of further Latin-script languages, such as Polish, Czech and Vietnamese, whatever their accents, and returns NA for a word in another script, where it returned 0.
  • The suggested model uses the stimuli’s condition column, where a lexical decision named a lexicality column the stimuli lack. Its note calls the random effects maximal only when they are, where it called them maximal in every factorial design.
  • The suggested model enters a matched design’s matched dimensions as centred covariates, where it had none, and gives items a condition slope whenever a Latin square ran, where categorisation had none.
  • For a continuous pair design, the suggested model crosses condition with the predictor, where it had no condition term.
  • For a user’s own registry entry with an openlexicon address, fetch_corpus() caches the download as a lexicon made by normalise_lexicon() with the entry’s columns and duplicates, where it cached the file as published, so the cached lexicon can differ.
  • OpenSesame response and question timeouts are written in whole milliseconds as declared, where 1,001 ms became 1,000, and a practice timeout is reported as ‘Too slow’, where it was scored as a wrong key.
  • The OpenSesame snippet inline_send_triggers.py sends only the condition code at the word’s onset, where the item code went first and delayed it, and inline_trigger_setup.py opens the serial port named at its top, where it took the first one found.
  • The en_rastle_repro example uses masked priming, where its prime had no forward mask, and it and en_andrews_repro run as lexical decisions with nonword fillers, where they had no nonwords.
  • The categorisation example adds 16 non-member foils as fillers, where pressing ‘yes’ on every trial scored perfectly.
  • The lexical-decision practice table presents ‘plang’ where it presented ‘plank’, an English word.

Changed interface

  • run_pipeline() refuses a probable design or schema key typo, such as n_per_conditon, where the key was ignored and the default count applied.
  • run_pipeline() and match_stimuli() refuse a matched design with a missing or empty match_on, where they paired the alphabetically first words.
  • A design’s name, language, font and condition names must be text, so a number or an unquoted no is refused, where a design with name: 2026 or language: no ran and named its files after 2026 or false.
  • A design whose name and language both hold only ASCII punctuation and spaces is refused, where it ran and wrote files named only by their suffix, such as _stimuli_R.csv and a hidden .osexp and .html.
  • lexsync requires jsonlite 1.8.7 or later, since 1.8.5 and 1.8.6 write datasheets that differ from the Python engine’s.
  • Matching refuses a condition left without a candidate complete on the matched dimensions, and mahalanobis refuses a pool with fewer than k + 2 complete rows for k dimensions.
  • resample_stimuli() and run_pipeline() refuse a resample.n_sets that is not a whole number of at least 1, where a fraction was truncated, a boolean or quoted number was taken as a count and zero gave an empty selection.
  • Counterbalancing refuses a counterbalance.optimise other than true or false, which balanced lists in Python only, and counterbalance.optimise: true on a Latin-square design that lists its own events. It refuses a factorial design with more lists than item sets.
  • A literal trigger code must be a whole number from 1 to 255, where 300 was sent as its low byte and 20.5 as 20. An unknown token such as conditon is refused, where send_trigger(NA) was written for OpenSesame.
  • A design that sends item codes with condition codes, or with its own codes from 40 to 239, and has more item sets than the codes left free is refused unless the schema sets triggers.allow_code_overlap: true.
  • A duration, fixed or read from an item column, must be present, finite and not negative, as must the lower bound of a jitter, where a blank or negative duration stopped the experiment or showed the stimulus for no time.
  • The exporters refuse a list or replicate that is not a whole number, and export_opensesame() refuses a non-numeric value in a numeric loop column.
  • A response event after a text event must share that event’s blocks unless it sets from: offset, and a YAML boolean response key, such as an unquoted yes, is refused.
  • A jsPsych page holding several versions runs nothing until its address gives ?participant=, ?version= or ?list=.
  • The result of export_experiments() gains files, the paths of every file written, so a loop over its values also gets that vector and its unlist() holds the PsychoPy script, the jsPsych page and version 1’s OpenSesame experiment twice.
  • With several versions, export_opensesame() and the opensesame path of export_experiments() give version 1’s experiment, where they gave the one experiment that held every version.
  • A design giving language_tag without language stops, where language_tag was read as language.
  • A design, schema or registry file that is not UTF-8 is refused, where it was cut short with a warning.
  • A norms entry with an unknown key is refused, where such a key was ignored, and so is a norms: block written as a mapping of named entries, which was accepted.
  • run_pipeline() refuses a reference_words list that is empty or holds a missing value.
  • lexsync refuses a lexsync.registry option or registry_path that names a missing file, where it read another registry, except that a missing registry_path failed with a connection error.
  • load_lexicon() refuses a non-numeric frequency column and a Zipf value outside 0 to 9, and a CSV header that names a column twice is refused. run_pipeline() refuses a design using n_syllables when a candidate lacks a syllable count.
  • describe_stimuli(), match_report() and match_report_continuous() refuse a dimension or grouping column the stimuli lack, where they returned a table of missing values with an n of 0.
  • Lexical-decision generation refuses words in a logographic script, such as Chinese, where it left them out.
  • run_all() refuses two designs that would write the same files, such as en-lexdec and en_lexdec.
  • run_pipeline() and run_all() default to schema_path = NULL, where they named the schema file they still read first when it exists.
  • Neither app runs a factorial design with nothing under ‘Match on’.
  • For a user’s own registry entry with an openlexicon address, fetch_corpus() refuses a download without a frequency column it can map, where it cached it as published.
  • fetch_corpus() refuses a corpus name holding a slash, backslash or colon before it reads the registry, where an edited registry could make it write outside the cache.
  • The en_priming_jitter item table items/priming_pairs_en_soa.csv names its per-trial column prime_ms, where it was soa_ms, since a 33 ms mask follows the prime.

Changed output

  • The OpenSesame loop table holds only numbers, adds lexsync_row and renames trial, list and set to lexsync_trial, lexsync_list and lexsync_set.
  • An OpenSesame experiment’s presented text, condition, block and answer move to a text table named after it, such as <base>_opensesame_text.csv, which must be copied with the experiment.
  • A design with several versions gets one OpenSesame experiment per version, such as <base>_list<k>.osexp, which warns and waits for space or escape when the subject number belongs to another version.
  • The jsPsych page saves <title>_v<version>.csv, or <title>_p<participant>_v<version>.csv when its address names a participant, where it saved <title>.csv. The PsychoPy script writes data/<base>_v<version>_<date>-<time>.csv, with _p<participant> before _v when a participant number is given.
  • In the jsPsych data, a response collected from its stimulus’s onset is recorded on that stimulus’s row, with lexsync_event ‘target’, where it had its own ‘response’ row. Every row gives the run’s version, replicate and list, with participant when known.
  • Launched without arguments, the PsychoPy experiment asks for the participant and the version in a start-up dialogue, even for a design with one version, where it started at once.
  • In a resampled design, the loop tables carry replicate and each version’s own copy of the practice and filler trials, and every loop table keeps each version’s trials together.
  • After a matching.shortfall: allow run falls short, the Methods paragraph states the number of items each condition holds, with the request beside it, where it stated the request.
  • The datasheet and Methods paragraph give the counterbalancing recipe and the number of lists that ran, where they inferred the recipe from the item source, calling a table-sourced lexical decision a Latin square, and gave counterbalance.lists, 1 by default.
  • The Methods paragraph and the Markdown datasheet’s realised-control table label the interval by the configured alpha, where they said 90% whatever the alpha, and the Methods paragraph gives a continuous design’s realised spreads and control windows in place of ‘near-constant’.
  • The Methods paragraph and Markdown datasheet say that the seed fixes only the trial order, where they tied the selection to the seed, and the datasheet no longer calls the selection free of item-selection bias.
  • The datasheet and Methods paragraph credit wordfreq only for the lexica lexsync ships, where a user’s own lexicon was described as wordfreq data. They name it by file name and checksum, and a fetched corpus by its registry citation.
  • The datasheet and Methods paragraph credit en_example.csv to wordfreq screened against SUBTLEX-US and state the screening rule, where they credited wordfreq alone.
  • The PsychoPy and OpenSesame experiments show instructions and wait for the space bar before the first trial, where they started at once, and jsPsych shows them in place of its general welcome, in English unless the design sets instructions.
  • When the trigger device cannot be opened, the PsychoPy and OpenSesame experiments say so on screen and wait for C under the default triggers.mode: auto, where they ran on without notice, and they log the mode on every trial.
  • The PsychoPy and jsPsych experiments treat fillers as main trials when they place pauses, where they paused before and after every filler. A design whose only blocks are practice, filler and main trials pauses once, where the practice trials end.
  • The Methods paragraph describes the realised control by its largest matched difference and then the equivalence tests, where it judged the control on the tests alone, and names large uncontrolled differences.
  • The Methods paragraph also says that each participant was presented one version, when responses were collected and, in a lexical decision, which key answered each condition.
  • The realised-control report covers every dimension lexsync knows and every pair of conditions. match_report() adds rows and the columns mean_diff and role after the existing ones and leaves out a dimension with no numeric value.
  • match_report_continuous() adds sd, sd_ratio, window_low and window_high, comparing the predictor’s spread with an even spread and each control’s with the pool’s.
  • A generated lexical decision’s report compares the words with the pseudowords on bigram frequency, N and OLD20, and build_lexdec_stimuli() returns base and edit_distance columns.
  • Datasheets use format 1.2, which adds fields for this release’s features, per-list counts and the schema’s path. design.n_per_condition gives the default applied when the design gives no count, where it was null.
  • The datasheet’s artefact list and the run log include the loop and text tables.
  • The datasheet’s realised-control entries give each dimension’s role as manipulated, controlled or uncontrolled, where every unmatched dimension was ‘manipulated/free’, and the Markdown table adds each row’s pair and raw difference.
  • An incomplete Latin-square rotation is reported in the run log, datasheet and Methods paragraph.
  • The Markdown datasheet and Methods paragraph round numbers half away from zero from the stored values, so some two-place values change, and print a TOST p to four places, with < 0.0001 for one that rounds to zero.
  • A generated design’s datasheet counts only the words the generator can use, where it counted the whole band.
  • A design whose name or language has non-ASCII characters gets a file stem ending in an eight-character checksum, given by design_stem(), where Chinese-named designs could share a stem and one with no ASCII letter or digit in either wrote hidden .osexp and .html files.
  • The apps’ download bundles hold the outputs under output/, where they sat at the archive’s root, and reproduce their own record without local paths. The PsychoPy and OpenSesame downloads are zip archives holding the tables those experiments load.
  • Both apps warn when ‘Match on’ names a dimension whose windows differ between conditions and label intervals by the configured alpha. They show each comparison’s role and raw difference and label each bar of the chart by dimension and pair.
  • Under the exported code, both apps say that the engines select byte-identical stimuli only when the run’s datasheet says so, where they said so under every matching method.
  • When no schema is named, run_pipeline() and run_all() say which one they use.
  • list_corpora() gives SUBTLEX-US the status ‘supported’, where it was ‘listed’, since fetch_corpus() can download it.
  • The run log notes settings that have no effect: an event’s onset_locked: false, a schema’s triggers.inter_trigger_ms and reference_words given for a generate or table design, which the datasheet no longer records as applied.
  • The run log notes a design in another language without its own instructions, a design whose instructions can only name its keys, a practice or filler answer the response mapping contradicts and a trial the lexical-decision default leaves without an answer.
  • lexsync reports a literal trigger code of 254 or 255, which the laboratory targets send as session markers, or one that equals a condition code or lies within the range of item codes the design sends.
  • The jsPsych page writes each trial’s numbers to 15 significant digits, where it kept four decimal places.
  • The datasheet records paths with forward slashes, where Windows paths kept their backslashes.
  • A block scalar (| or >) that ends a design, schema or registry file keeps its final line break, as in the Python engine, so a description written that way ends with one in the datasheet.

New features

  • validate_design() checks a design’s keys and values, and run_pipeline() calls it before anything is selected or written.
  • counterbalance.max_run caps runs of one condition, or of one value of a column named in counterbalance.run_on, in the trial order, and refuses only a limit no order can meet (van Casteren & Davis, 2006). It is off by default.
  • counterbalance.orders: m gives each list m trial orders, each with its own practice order, which participants take by participant number. The loop tables gain order_1 to order_m, and OpenSesame gets one experiment per version and order. The PsychoPy and jsPsych data record the order each run used.
  • counterbalance.scale: mad balances lists in units of each dimension’s mean absolute deviation, so a dimension’s weight does not depend on where its scale starts. The default stays mean.
  • counterbalance.incomplete: error, in the design or the schema, refuses an incomplete Latin-square rotation.
  • counterbalance.recipe (factorial or latin_square_target) overrides the counterbalancing recipe of the design’s paradigm.
  • normalise_lexicon() turns a delimited corpus file into a lexicon, deriving Zipf values from frequencies per million and summing a form’s rows under a registry entry’s duplicates: sum. fetch_corpus("subtlex_us") downloads and normalises SUBTLEX-US, and a registry entry may name a derived file, already normalised, to fetch instead.
  • masked_priming presents a forward mask of hash marks, a lower-case prime and an upper-case target (Forster & Davis, 1984). A text event’s case sets the case shown, and a mask’s length_of sets its length.
  • A design sets its instruction text with instructions, and response_mapping and rotate_mapping_by_list set the key that answers each condition and rotate the keys across lists.
  • items.generation.exclude lists word forms a generated pseudoword must not equal, from files or fetched corpora, and generate_pseudowords() and build_lexdec_stimuli() take them as exclude. The datasheet records each list with its checksum.
  • exclude_words lists words a design leaves out of its candidates, inline or in a file, and the datasheet records the list with its checksum.
  • en_v2.csv, a screened English lexicon in the repository, marks the forms absent from SUBTLEX-US or seldom written in lower case (Brysbaert & New, 2009) and counts N and OLD20 over the unmarked forms, keeping the unscreened values in n_density_raw and old20_raw. pool_filters: {nonstandard: [0, 0]} keeps the unmarked forms.
  • The es_lexdec example generates a Spanish lexical decision and checks its pseudowords against wordfreq’s Spanish word list.
  • In the schema, triggers.mode: hardware stops an experiment whose trigger device cannot be opened, and triggers.mode: mock prints the codes without trying it. triggers.backend: serial sends each code as one byte to triggers.serial_port at triggers.baudrate, 115200 by default.
  • A design can use a derived dimension (n_density, old20 or bigram_freq) in define_by, pool_filters, counterbalance.balance_on or a continuous design’s predictor or controls, and run_pipeline() computes any the lexicon lacks.
  • A lexicon or pool may mark the forms that make up the neighbourhood reference with a reference_member column of 0 and 1.
  • The PsychoPy script takes --participant, --version or --list, and the jsPsych page reads ?participant=, ?version= or ?list= from its address. Both refuse a list when the versions span several replicates.

Minor improvements

  • When no schema is named and none is found where 0.1.1 looked, run_pipeline() tries a schema.yaml beside the design and run_all() tries config/schema.yaml in the working directory. Both then fall back to the schema bundled with the package, where they stopped.
  • run_pipeline() refuses a missing name or language, an unsafe name or font, a bad trigger address or response key and a repeated condition name before anything is written, where these failed later, some at export after four files had been written.
  • assign_triggers() gains events and schema, which export_experiments() passes so that item codes avoid the design’s other codes.
  • build_datasheet() gains counterbalance_check, input_normalisation, generation_exclude, exclusions, zipf_derivation and trial_order, which run_pipeline() passes for the format 1.2 fields.
  • match_report() gains roles, a function giving each comparison’s role, which run_pipeline() derives from the design, and match_report_continuous() gains audit, the selector’s record of the control windows, which it reads from the stimuli by default.
  • match_stimuli() and select_continuous_stimuli() refuse n_per_condition: 0 as not a positive whole number, where they failed with an unrelated error.
  • optimal matching runs much faster on large pools.
  • fetch_corpus() refusals name the registry they read and say when an entry registers no download address. It explains that the Python package builds a wordfreq lexicon, where it said the language was not in the registry.
  • A norms entry that is not a mapping, such as a bare file name, is refused as needing a path, where it failed with R’s own error.
  • The Shiny method selector carries the Streamlit app’s note on mahalanobis and optimal, and each app removes a run’s folder once the next run’s results or an error replace its results.

Fixes

  • Generated OpenSesame experiments no longer pass stimulus text through OpenSesame’s variable store, which evaluates it, so a shared item table can no longer run code on the presenting machine.
  • The jsPsych page loads jsPsych, its keyboard plugin and its stylesheet from unpkg with Subresource Integrity, so a browser refuses a modified copy.
  • A resampled design with filler trials runs, where it stopped with an error.
  • Generated OpenSesame experiments run with words such as ‘nan’ and ‘infinity’ in the stimuli, where these could stop an OpenSesame 4 session.
  • A factorial design with a key whose name begins with another key’s, such as continuous_notes, runs, where it stopped.
  • Joint matching over more than 1,200 candidates on a dimension with missing values no longer fails.
  • list_corpora() and fetch_corpus() read the bundled registry under the C locale, where they failed.
  • Both apps leave out a factor whose bound is not a number, where they stopped with an error.
  • Both apps’ exported command lines quote the design file’s name and run in cmd.exe and Windows PowerShell.
  • The Streamlit app’s exported Rscript command passes the outdir that run_pipeline() requires.
  • lexsync installs the licence notice for its CC BY-SA lexica as COPYRIGHTS, so binary installations carry it.

Deprecated

  • A design or schema key lexsync does not read is noted in the run log and will be refused in a later release. Annotations belong in description or a key beginning x_.

Documentation

  • The experiments vignette is substantially extended, with new sections on when a response is collected, instructions and the response mapping, trial orders, running a counterbalanced experiment and checking the timing with a photodiode. The matching vignette adds a section on choosing and screening a lexicon, which says that the wordfreq lexica hold names, acronyms and other non-standard forms, and covers ties between equally close candidates. The reproducibility vignette sets out the CSV and YAML input contracts and the file names.
  • The experiments vignette says that every participant given a list and trial order meets the practice trials in one fixed order, where it said that the practice trials were shuffled so that participants meet them in different orders.
  • The documentation says that a continuous design spreads its items over the predictor’s ranks, so the selection follows the pool’s distribution, and that the tolerance windows trim the controls’ tails without holding them constant, which the matching vignette and the 0.1.0 notes misstated.
  • The matching vignette says that a generated pseudoword is a non-word only relative to the reference words, so it can be a real word too rare for the lexicon, such as crier or pall, where it said it could not be a real word.
  • The experiments vignette says that item trigger codes follow the code-point order of the set labels, so that, with sets 1 to 20, set 10 is 41 and set 2 is 51, and that they are decoded through the loop table.
  • The schema’s comments say that the trigger settings, and the presentation settings other than font, apply to every design run with the schema, where they said that a design could override them.
  • The Get started vignette says that the timing keys reach every fixation, every text event whose trigger is condition and every blank, but not an event with a per-trial duration block, where it named only the fixation, critical-word and inter-stimulus durations.
  • The vignettes say that a pool filter given two numbers is an inclusive range whatever the column, that standardised_euclidean is the one default matching method and that list balancing runs at most counterbalance.max_passes passes, 500 by default.
  • resample_stimuli() says that its selections match the other engine’s only under standardised_euclidean and joint.
  • The documentation calls the 0.5 equivalence bound a convention, where the schema and the help page of tost_equiv() credited it to Lakens (2017), and the quick starts in the README and the Get started vignette use 60 items per condition, where they used 15, too few for any varying dimension to pass the equivalence test.
  • The corpus registry no longer gives the SUBTLEX-US and SUBTLEX-DE log-count columns, or a SUBTLEX-CH column that does not exist, as the source of freq_zipf.
  • The app vignette and both apps’ tolerance panels give the frequency k of González Alonso et al. (2025) as 0.1111111111111111, since 0.111 gives a window narrower than a ninth of a standard deviation.

lexsync 0.1.1

CRAN release: 2026-09-25

  • assign_triggers() gains a conditions argument that fixes the order of the condition codes, and export_experiments() gains one that defaults to the order of the design’s conditions. The codes used to follow the order in which the conditions first appeared in the counterbalanced trials, so a different seed could swap them, and low_frequency was 101 in a design that lists high_frequency first. The pipeline now passes the design’s order, followed by any other condition in the order the item source lists it, so the first condition the design lists is 101. The condition codes of 12 of the 21 demonstration designs change with it. assign_triggers() called without conditions behaves as before.
  • cohens_d_ci() uses the large-sample standard error of d, sqrt(1/nx + 1/ny + d^2 / (2 * (nx + ny))) (Hedges & Olkin, 1985; Borenstein et al., 2009). It left out the d^2 term, which treated the pooled SD as known and made the interval on a manipulated dimension far too narrow. In the English frequency contrast, d = 5.27 had the interval [5.01, 5.53] and now has [4.72, 5.83]. A matched control, whose d is near zero, moves by at most 0.002 across the 21 demonstration designs, and no d, TOST p-value or verdict changes. The comparisons, datasheets and run logs of the designs with a manipulated dimension change with it. No stimulus moves.
  • match_report() documents the direction of its signed statistics. cohens_d and its interval are the reference (first) condition’s mean minus the mean of the condition in that row, and var_ratio is that condition’s variance over the reference’s.
  • New lexsync_cache_clear() removes a fetched corpus from the cache, together with any partial download of it, or with no argument removes the whole cache. It returns the paths it removed, invisibly.
  • lexsync_cache_dir() only reports the cache’s path. It created the directory on every call, so asking where the cache was left an empty directory behind. fetch_corpus() now creates the cache when a download into it starts, once the registry entry and its URL have been accepted, so a refused call writes nothing. That download begins by deleting any .part sidecar in the cache that has gone a day without a write. An interrupt or a process that died mid-transfer leaves one behind, and no handler removes it. A younger sidecar may belong to a download still running in another session, so it is left alone. A dest of the caller’s choosing behaves as before.
  • citation("lexsync") gives the DOI that CRAN assigned to the package, https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.lexsync, with the CRAN page as its URL. The 0.1.0 build on CRAN predates the DOI and gives the repository’s address. The entry names CRAN as its publisher, and its text version is the APA reference for software: author, year, title, version, “[Computer software]”, CRAN and the DOI.
  • The tests no longer take another package’s sources for the lexsync repository. CRAN’s Linux hosts check each package beside the unpacked sources of the others, and the test holding the bundled templates to the repository’s templates/ directory found the unrelated ‘templates’ package there and failed. A test that compares the package with repository files now accepts a root only if it holds lexsync’s own DESCRIPTION under R_workflow/ and the Python package beside it, and skips on CRAN.
  • Suggests now asks for testthat 3.1.8, the first release whose local_mocked_bindings() can replace an imported function, as the corpus download tests do with download.file().

lexsync 0.1.0

CRAN release: 2026-09-22

  • First release: multilingual corpus access, parallel multidimensional matching, counterbalancing, item resampling, deterministic pseudoword generation, and generation of hardware-timed PsychoPy, OpenSesame and jsPsych experiments. The R and Python engines select byte-identical stimuli, and every run ships a materials datasheet (provenance, checksums, realised control) and a pre-registration template.
  • See the top-level CHANGELOG.md for the full, cross-language history and the planned methodological roadmap.

Changes made before the release

These notes follow the package through its development up to the release, so they describe each change against the state it replaced.

  • The package now declares Depends: R (>= 4.0.0). tools::R_user_dir does not exist before 4.0.0, and round()’s post-4.0 algorithm shapes artefact bytes, so an older R would fail obscurely or write different bytes without complaint.
  • The published median goes through the exact reductions. describe_stimuli() was the one reduction still on stats::median, which averages the two middle values through mean()’s long-double accumulator while the Python engine reduced through numpy. Both engines now sort and take the exact middle, with (a + b) / 2 in plain double arithmetic for even n, and regenerating every design moved no byte. Reproducibility and parity claimed that every reduction shared one compensated-summation algorithm, which the median never did, and now describes the sort-and-middle rule beside it.
  • The dead half of the two-shortest-forms CSV guard now fires. Between 2^49 and 1e15 two one-decimal strings can round-trip to the same double, and the R check derived its digit count from a 15-digit format that never shows a fractional digit there, so R accepted values (844424930131968.2 among them) that the Python writer refused. R now refuses exactly the same values, and the change only adds refusals.
  • A condition without define_by selects identically in both engines. This engine always fell back to the whole pool. The Python engine crashed with a bare KeyError on the same design and now mirrors the fallback, pinned by twin tests.
  • A pair design’s tolerance-window relaxation reaches the run log and datasheet. The continuous-pairs selector’s re-expansion dropped the audit in both engines, so a relaxed window left no trace outside the console. No shipped pair design relaxes, so no committed artefact changed.
  • INTER_TRIGGER_S is substituted through %.17g like its neighbours in the generated PsychoPy script. It used as.character(), whose rendering of a non-integer quotient differs from Python’s str(). The shipped default still renders “0.01”, so no committed experiment byte moved.
  • The counterbalancing hash keys convert to UTF-8 before hashing, as hash_unit() always has, so a latin1-marked condition read from a user’s CSV can no longer rank by different digests in the two engines.
  • The command-line wrapper reports which copy of the package it loaded. R_workflow/run_pipeline.R prefers an installed lexsync over the edited sources, so edits silently did nothing until a reinstall. It now states the loaded copy and the remedy on stderr at startup.
  • The Shiny app writes its design YAML with LF endings through a binary connection (the datasheet hashes that file into design_sha256, which must not depend on the operating system), and its parity caption now matches the keyed-hash guarantee: the engines produce byte-identical stimuli and trial order, where the caption used to promise only the stimuli. The Python engine’s twin fixes land in the same release: its writer refuses 16-digit integer columns as this engine always has, its scalar rounder passes an overflowing scale through, and run_pipeline(verbose = FALSE) keeps its console silent.
  • A selection that cannot honour n_per_condition is now an error. Every selector used to clip the request to the available pool and said so at most through a verbose message, while the datasheet and the generated Methods text kept stating the requested n. The new matching: shortfall policy defaults to error, and allow accepts the shrink. Its sibling matching: on_insufficient_tolerance (default relax) can likewise turn the silent tolerance-window widening into a refusal, and a relaxation that does happen is now recorded in the run log and the datasheet (selection.window_relaxations), where before it was only narrated to the console. No committed design experiences either condition.
  • joint and optimal matching can no longer select the same word twice. With overlapping condition windows a word could be paired with itself at zero cost, or mirrored across two sets, appearing in both conditions. Both matchers now track used words as the anchored matcher always has, and every matcher asserts its output holds each word at most once. Every committed design has disjoint conditions, and those select identically, byte for byte.
  • The item-table loader refuses missing cells in both engines. A blank condition reached Python’s hash-key guard as the string “nan” and passed the very check built to refuse it, a blank item cell turned numeric identifiers into “1.0”, and R failed on the same table with a bare “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”. Missingness is now checked before any coercion, item is read as text, empties after trimming and duplicated item-and-condition rows are refused, and both engines say the same thing.
  • Cohen’s d no longer reports perfect balance for two unequal constant vectors. The standardised difference is undefined when the pooled SD is zero and the means differ, so it is now reported as missing. The old 0 with CI [0, 0] contradicted the TOST verdict on the same row.
  • The datasheet’s Methods prose follows the recorded verdicts. The claim of being “within the 0.5-SD equivalence bound” was printed for any controlled dimension with a confidence interval, even where the datasheet’s own JSON recorded equivalent: false. The sentence is now conditional on the stored verdicts, prints the signed worst difference and the configurable bound, and the analysis note names the suggested formula as lme4 syntax, where it used to imply that statsmodels accepts it. The datasheet also gains the SHA-256 of the design and schema, the pairwise matchers’ candidate cap and whether it fired, the equivalence bound tested against, and the yaml, stringi and operating-system entries the environment record omitted.
  • A continuous block now works over a supplied pool, and two silent table-mode gaps are refusals. source: pool reaches the continuous selector (it previously fell through to the conditions matcher and crashed). A continuous table without members is an error now, as is pool_filters on a plain table design, where each used to do nothing silently while the provenance recorded otherwise. Misspelt pool_filters or define_by columns, duplicate condition names, reversed or non-finite ranges, negative tolerances and non-integer n are likewise refusals now.
  • Selection-path rounding goes through the shared decimal rule (.round_dp and a new vectorised numpy twin), replacing a pairing of R’s round() with numpy’s, two rounders the project measured to disagree at boundaries. Regenerating all 21 designs moved no stimulus, report or experiment byte. A custom norm named in match_on now also reaches the descriptives, comparisons and realised-control record, which previously listed only the built-in dimensions.
  • A design file could execute code on the machine that ran it. A design is meant to be shared, and the recipient runs it and then opens the generated PsychoPy script, OpenSesame experiment or jsPsych page. Stimulus text was always safe: it travels in the loop-table CSV the experiment reads at run time. Design metadata was not. The name, language label, font, parallel-port address and the column names on jitter and feedback events were substituted straight into code and markup positions, so a quote or an angle bracket there stopped being text and became syntax, and a crafted design could run arbitrary code on a lab machine or in the origin of a hosted browser study. Both engines now validate these values, under one rule that leaves every legitimate value byte-identical. A port address must be an address, a column name must be an identifier, and a stated language_tag is shape-checked before it is used. Escaping them correctly would have taken three rules per engine. .pyq() escapes newlines now as well: an .osexp is line-oriented, so a raw newline closed the inline-script block and let the rest of the value start a new top-level item. Pinned by test-injection.R. No generated artefact changed. Adversarially attacking that fix then found four ways through it, all now closed and pinned. The largest: a response event’s keys were joined into OpenSesame’s set allowed_responses "a;b" with no validation at all, and that is one line of a line-oriented format, so a key holding a double quote closed the string, a newline ended the line, and the rest of the value became new top-level items in the experiment, including an inline_script whose body OpenSesame runs. Keys are validated now. The shape guards were also anchored with $, which in both Python’s re and R’s PCRE matches just before a final newline, so a port address ending in one passed the check. They are anchored at end-of-string now. A scalar keys: space or blocks: practice was iterated character by character in Python and kept whole in R, so one design gave two different allowed-response lists and a block-restricted event ran everywhere in one engine and nowhere in the other. And R’s HTML escape did not cover U+2028/U+2029, which end a line in JavaScript but are not ASCII controls: Python escaped them, R did not, so the same design produced different bytes and R’s <script> was a syntax error before ES2019.
  • A browser experiment could score a feedback screen against the previous trial’s keypress. The jsPsych feedback screen looked up “the last row marked scoreable”, which is that trial’s response only when the trial has one. An event may be restricted to a block, so a design running the response event in one block and feedback in another leaves a trial with no response row of its own, and the screen then reported a verdict computed from an earlier trial’s key. Each trial’s rows now carry its own identifier and the screen matches on it. The generated HTML changed for all 21 designs. No stimulus selection changed.
  • A large number in a user’s own column was written differently by the two engines. write_csv_utf8() reproduced readr’s format for small magnitudes and left the top end alone, since nothing lexsync computes reaches it. Nothing lexsync computes does. A joined norm table, a supplied pool or an item table carries whatever columns the user has, and those go straight into the stimuli CSV, so the guarantee held for the shipped designs and failed silently for the user’s own data. readr’s layout above 1e15 could not be reproduced in Python, which writes 1.5e16 as 15e15, the largest double as 17976931348623157e292, and the double nearest 5e22 as 4.9999999999999996e+22. Both engines now refuse such a value and name the column. One engine accepting it would leave the two writing different bytes. A value with two equally short decimal forms is refused for the same reason. Everything verified to render identically, across 465 values compared against readr’s own output, writes as before.
  • A generated OpenSesame experiment with a feedback event or a blocks: restriction would not run. The emitter wrote unicode(...), a Python 2 builtin that OpenSesame’s Python 3 inline workspace does not provide, so the experiment died with NameError on the first trial. It also passed None as a var.get() default, which OpenSesame cannot distinguish from no default, so it raises where it should return. Both are fixed, both spellings are now pinned by a test, and a feedback event with no preceding response or question is refused at generation time. Left to run time, that one design error would surface as three different failures, one per target.
  • Reported statistics are rounded by an arithmetic definition both engines compute identically, because no pairing of built-ins agreed. Measured over 210,000 values, including every three-decimal halfway case in range, R’s round() disagrees with Python’s builtin, Python’s builtin disagrees with numpy’s, and even R’s sprintf("%.3f") disagrees with Python’s "%.3f" on 274 of them. Some values move by one in the last published digit. No selection changes.
  • A hash-key component that cannot be rendered identically in both engines is now refused rather than hashed. A blank condition cell, a routine data error neither reader rejects, rendered "NA" in R and "nan" in Python, so the two engines produced different trial orders from the same design, reproducibly and with nothing to signal it. Booleans get a pinned spelling and are still accepted.
  • The overlap-cap centroid in the joint and optimal matchers goes through the compensated reduction. The cap does fire on shipped designs, so it decides which candidates reach matching. It was verified to change no design’s selection.
  • R CMD check --as-cran is clean: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 note (the standard new-submission note). Fixed on the way: three undocumented arguments on select_continuous_stimuli(), an unqualified utils::head(), and the package’s only example, which called an unexported function from inside \dontrun{} and so could never have worked if a user copied it. The package now has executable, offline examples, and cran-comments.md no longer misstates the check result.
  • Three factual corrections. The SUBTLEX-PT registry entry cited a DOI that resolves to an unrelated psychometrics paper. The matching vignette put Zipf 7 at a thousand occurrences per million where the correct figure is ten thousand, contradicting its own lower anchor. A design comment attributed “840-prime materials” to Rastle et al. (2004), a figure that appears nowhere in that paper.
  • A design may declare practice: and fillers: item tables. Those trials are presented but not analysed, so the stimuli file and the reports are written from the main rows while the generated experiments run every trial. Practice comes first. Fillers are interleaved with the main trials, because a block of fillers at the end is not a filler but a second block a participant can tell apart. A design declaring neither is unaffected, down to not gaining a block column.
  • A feedback trial event, and a blocks: key that restricts any event to named blocks. Together these confine feedback to practice, which is the usual arrangement: feedback teaches the mapping, and would contaminate the reaction times it is measuring. Implemented for PsychoPy, OpenSesame and jsPsych alike. The PsychoPy runner now returns the pressed key so it can be scored, and each runner pauses at a block boundary.
  • The Python engine embedded a bare NaN in the generated jsPsych experiment where a trial had no value for a field another block supplies (a main-block trial in a design whose practice items carry an answer). That is not valid JSON, and the R engine dropped the key instead, so the two engines’ experiments differed. Both now drop it.
  • The generated artefacts were not byte-identical across the engines, and the parity test could not see it. It read both CSVs back with a parser and compared the values, under which 1 and 1.0 are the same number. Thirteen of the 18 shipped designs differed byte for byte while the gate stayed green. Three differences were serialisation (a whole number written 1 and 1.0, a boolean written FALSE and False, a small value written 9e-4 and 0.0009) and one was not: two reported means differed in the last decimal published, because numpy sums pairwise and R’s mean() does not. Every reduction in the package now uses one compensated-summation algorithm written out in both engines, whose agreement follows from IEEE-754 and no longer from measurement. The writers agree on every value, and the artefacts are now compared as bytes. No R golden moved, because R’s two-pass mean was already the correctly-rounded one.
  • A response key coded f was silently turned into FALSE. readr reads a column whose values are all f, t, T or F as logical, while pandas keeps the string, so an item table using the commonest two-choice key pair had its correct answer corrupted in one engine. Item tables now read the condition label and the paradigm’s presented fields as text in both engines.
  • jsonlite’s default of four digits was truncating the datasheet: a design declaring tolerance_k: 0.1111111111111111 had it recorded as 0.1111, which does not reproduce the run the record exists to describe. The JSON is now written at full display precision, and the Python engine writes the same precision.
  • New paradigm categorisation: a category cue, then the word to judge against it, with answer holding the correct response key so the data are scoreable. Counterbalanced by Latin-square rotation, so a participant never sees the same target twice.
  • counterbalance.optimise (off by default) assigns item sets to lists so the lists are equated on the declared dimensions, where the old deal went by set rank. The search is a deterministic integer descent with a keyed-hash tie-break, so it uses no random number generator and both engines produce the same assignment. balance_lists() is exported.
  • New item source pool: a supplied word list goes through the matcher without having to masquerade as a corpus lexicon. load_pool() is exported. The neighbourhood dimensions are computed against the lexicon’s words, because a word’s neighbours are its neighbours in the language.
  • A design may name norm tables in a norms: block. They are joined onto the lexicon before the candidate pool is built, so a semantic dimension the corpus does not carry (concreteness, age of acquisition, valence) can be filtered on, matched on or spanned like any other. No norm data is bundled. Every joined table is recorded in the materials datasheet with its checksum and its per-column coverage, because a norm table can supply the very variable a design manipulates.
  • Datasheet version 1.1. It adds materials_source$norms and, for a pair-keyed design, a relational block naming the members, the pair count, the member lexicon and its checksum, and the member-level dimensions separately from the relational ones. selection$cross_engine no longer reports “n/a (user-supplied items)” for a pair-keyed continuous design: that design does perform a selection, and it is byte-identical across engines.
  • merge_norms() returns the lexicon with the norm columns appended, in the lexicon’s own row and column order. It previously used merge(), which hoists the join column to position 1 where pandas keeps the left frame’s order, so the two engines disagreed on column order whenever on was not already first. The join key is now case- and whitespace-folded on the lexicon’s side too, where only the norm table’s was folded before: a lexicon holding Dog used to match nothing and leave an all-NA dimension. A norm column whose name already exists on the lexicon is now an error. Renaming it to frequency.x / frequency.y, as merge() did, left the matched dimension under a name nothing looks for.
  • write_datasheet() and write_run_log() now write LF on every platform. They used a text-mode connection, so on Windows the datasheet, its Markdown rendering and the Markdown run log came out CRLF while the Python engine’s twins were LF. The datasheet is the provenance record. Its bytes no longer depend on the machine that built it.
  • add_pair_overlap() and resolve_trial_timing() are now exported in fact as well as in the documentation. Both were marked for export and documented, but the NAMESPACE had not been regenerated, so library(lexsync) did not make them available.
  • The materials datasheet now reports the candidate-pool size per condition (selection transparency, making item-selection bias auditable) and a suggested crossed mixed-model formula that guards against the language-as-fixed-effect fallacy.
  • Browser (jsPsych) experiments gain a welcome/instructions screen, per-row item metadata (condition, item id, list), and a completion screen that saves the collected data as a CSV download.
  • The realised-control report and datasheet gain a variance ratio per dimension, a distributional balance check that complements Cohen’s d and TOST.
  • Wuggy-style subsyllabic pseudoword generation (opt-in items.generation.method: subsyllabic): whole onset/nucleus/coda constituents are swapped for attested same-role, same-length alternatives, preserving syllabic structure and length. Byte-identical across engines, and the default letter-substitution generator is unchanged.
  • Continuous (non-dichotomised) design mode: declare a continuous block and select_continuous_stimuli() spans a predictor’s range evenly while holding the controls near-constant, with predictor-control correlations and a regression suggested-model in the datasheet. Byte-identical across the R and Python engines.
  • Two new matching methods: mahalanobis (a covariance-aware distance that down-weights correlated dimensions) and optimal (a globally optimal assignment for two-condition designs, using the suggested clue package). Unlike the default methods, these use a covariance inverse and an assignment solver, so the R and Python engines agree closely but not byte-for-byte on them.
  • An unknown matching.method, and a candidate pool too small for the requested n_per_condition, now raise an actionable error. Each used to fall back silently, to a default method or to a short set. The Python engine raises the same message, and code that relied on the old fallback will now stop.
  • stringi is a new hard dependency (Imports). The canonical word key is case-folded with ICU at the root locale, so the key no longer depends on the machine’s locale and matches the Python engine byte for byte. shiny, bslib, DT and zip are new Suggests, for the Shiny app.
  • Ten functions are newly exported, matching the Python package’s public surface: PARADIGMS(), build_datasheet(), build_lexdec_stimuli(), count_syllables(), generate_pseudowords(), make_pseudoword(), methods_paragraph(), required_fields(), resolve_events() and write_datasheet().
  • tost_equiv() now defaults to bound_d = 0.5, the value the Python engine already used. The R default was 0.4, so the equivalence bound is wider and a comparison is easier to declare equivalent. Reported verdicts can change for the same data.
  • describe_stimuli() now orders rows by each group’s first appearance, matching pandas. This changes the row order of generated descriptives.
  • OpenSesame experiments now present trials in the seeded counterbalanced order. The order was previously randomised again at run time, so what ran was not what the pipeline generated and recorded.
  • Breaking change: trial order within each counterbalancing list now comes from a seeded, keyed-hash shuffle shared with the Python engine. Each row is ranked by the SHA-256 digest of seed|replicate|list|set|condition, a tuple that identifies the trial uniquely under either counterbalancing recipe, so the permutation is a pure function of the design: byte-identical from both engines on any platform, and different for every seed. Previously the order was drawn from sample(), which could never match numpy’s generator for the same seed, so the trial lists were the one engine-specific artefact. All 75 generated experiment files across the 15 designs bundled at the time are now byte-identical across the engines, and the parity gate now compares the trial column of the stimuli CSVs. Stimulus selection, pairing and lists are unchanged, but every design’s trial order changes relative to the previous artefacts. The package no longer uses R’s random-number generator at all, so a seeded run cannot perturb the calling script’s random stream and there is no RNG state to save or restore.
  • merge_norms() preserves the lexicon’s row order, and participant_table() crosses factors in expand.grid() order in both engines.
  • Datasheets record the tolerance windows and pseudoword generator that ran, filter dimensions as the Python engine does, and report the installed package version they were built by.
  • match_stimuli() raises where it used to re-pick an already-used row, when a relaxed window re-admits candidates missing a matched dimension. Such a candidate has no defined distance and is never assigned, yet it still counted towards the pool-size guard. An NA-depleted pool could therefore pass the guard and go on to emit the same word in several sets.
  • match_stimuli() and select_continuous_stimuli() no longer select an all-NA row when the tolerance window is NA (an anchor of a single item gives sd = NA). An undecided comparison now resolves to FALSE, as it does in Python, so the window is relaxed and a real word is selected.
  • The generated PsychoPy script, OpenSesame experiment and jsPsych page are now byte-identical to the Python engine’s, trial lists included (see the keyed-hash shuffle entry above).
  • Selected stimuli are unchanged for all 15 designs bundled at the time.
  • Every vignette now turns console colour off and fixes the console width while it renders. pkgdown passes the calling terminal’s colour support into its build subprocess, so a coloured message or error would otherwise reach the reader as escape sequences in the middle of the text.
